newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Japan rejects U.S. claims in WTO photofilm row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Japan rejects U.S. claims in WTO photofilm row.

text.p: Japan told a World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute panel on Thursday U.S. charges that it deliberately skews its domestic market to keep out foreign photo-film products had no basis in fact.

The Japanese stance in the row -- which pits the two governments against each other on behalf of Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd and Eastman Kodak Co -- was set out in a formal submission to the three-man panel.

"The Japanese film and paper markets are open to imports," said a detailed document delivered to the panel by Tokyo officials. "Success in the Japanese market depends simply upon the efforts of private companies."
Fuji has consistently argued that Kodak has failed to win more customers in Japan through lack of attention to pricing policy and to what Japanese consumers want.

In Tokyo, a senior Trade Ministry official, in remarks echoed by Japanese diplomats in Geneva, said the U.S. argument set out in a 200-page submission on February 20, "is both factually baseless and legally groundless."

He said Japan had never taken any action which violated world trade accords supervised by the WTO or which effectively nullified agreements on lowering tariff barriers by creating other obstacles to open commerce.
The action was launched by Washington in the trade body in June last year after years of complaint by Kodak.

The panel, whose members were appointed in December last year, would normally be expected to deliver its findings by the middle of June. But diplomats say the complicated nature of the case could cause a delay of several weeks or even months.

Whatever the outcome, an appeal is almost certain and under WTO procedures a final ruling by the trade watchdog's Dispute Settlement Body -- on which all 130 member countries can sit -- might not come until well into 1998.
When the U.S. presented its own case to the panel, Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky argued that Japan set domestic regulations to shield Fuji from import competition.

Kodak, which holds 70 per cent of the U.S. domestic market but only nine per cent in Japan, says that for two decades it has lost up to $5.6 billion annually in potential sales to Japanese consumers because of unfair marketing rules.
Fuji, which has around 67 per cent of its home market, counters that it faces distribution barriers in the United States, where it holds 12 per cent of the market.

In a statement issued in Geneva on Thursday, Fuji's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Minoru Ohnishi said the arguments presented by Japanese officials to the panel amounted to an "overwhelming case" against the U.S. complaint.

Washington, Ohnishi said, was aiming "to impose its distorted views on the Japanese photographic market to force a greater market share for Kodak". Fuji, he added, was confident that the panel would find in Japan's favour.
"Once the case is decided, we at Fujifilm look forward to returning to the serious business of competing in the marketplace, without government intervention ," he said.
The United States argues that the dispute is not a fight between two competitor companies but a normal trade dispute between two countries.
"This is a case about classic protectionism accomplished through novel means," Barshefsky said in February.
